hmmt-feb-2006-geo-01.title: Complete to a rectangle
hmmt-feb-2006-geo-01.body:
All angles are $135^\circ$. Extend $AB,CD,EF,GH$ to form a rectangle: let $X=GH\cap AB$, $Y=AB\cap CD$, $Z=CD\cap EF$, $W=EF\cap GH$. The cut-off corners are isosceles right triangles with hypotenuses $BC=2$, $DE=4$, $FG=2$, so $BY=YC=\sqrt2$, $DZ=ZE=2\sqrt2$, $FW=WG=\sqrt2$.

The rectangle has $WX=YZ=YC+CD+DZ=3+3\sqrt2$ and $XY=ZW=ZE+EF+FW=2+3\sqrt2$. Then $HX=XA=XY-AB-BY=1+2\sqrt2$, so $AH=\sqrt2\,HX=4+\sqrt2$, and $GH=WX-WG-HX=2$.

The perimeter is $1+2+3+4+2+2+2+(4+\sqrt2)=20+\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $20+\sqrt2$**

hmmt-feb-2006-geo-02.title: Angle bisector
hmmt-feb-2006-geo-02.body:
The right angle is at $B$, so $BP$ bisects it. By the angle bisector theorem $\frac{AB}{BC}=\frac{AP}{PC}=\frac12$; write $BC=2x$, $AB=x$. Then $5x^2=AC^2=9$, and the area is $\frac12\cdot x\cdot2x=x^2=\frac95$.

**Answer: 9/5**

hmmt-feb-2006-geo-03.title: Power of a point
hmmt-feb-2006-geo-03.body:
Take the order $X,P,Q,Y$ on the line and let $PX=x$, $QY=y$. Power of $P$: $x(27+y)=AP\cdot PB=6\cdot5=30$. Power of $Q$: $y(27+x)=CQ\cdot QD=7\cdot12=84$. Subtracting, $27(y-x)=54$, so $y=x+2$. Then $x(29+x)=30$, so $x=1$ (the other root $-30$ is impossible), $y=3$, and $XY=1+27+3=31$.

**Answer: 31**

hmmt-feb-2006-geo-04.title: Split the area
hmmt-feb-2006-geo-04.body:
Let $O$ be the center of the semicircle (on $BC$) and $r$ its radius. Since the semicircle is tangent to $AB$ and $AC$, the distances from $O$ to these lines are $r$, so $[ABC]=[AOB]+[AOC]=\frac12(AB+AC)r=\frac52r$.

By Heron's formula with $s=\frac92$: $[ABC]=\sqrt{\frac92\cdot\frac52\cdot\frac32\cdot\frac12}=\frac{3\sqrt{15}}4$. Hence $r=\frac{3\sqrt{15}}{10}$, and the area is $\frac12\pi r^2=\frac12\pi\cdot\frac{135}{100}=\frac{27\pi}{40}$.

**Answer: $\frac{27\pi}{40}$**

hmmt-feb-2006-geo-05.title: Coordinates
hmmt-feb-2006-geo-05.body:
Since $CB+BF=1+2=3=CF$, the point $B$ lies on segment $CF$, with $F=3B$ as a position vector from $C$. Put $C=(0,0)$, $A=(5,0)$. From $BC=1$ and $AB^2=20$ we get $B=\left(\frac35,\frac45\right)$, so $F=\left(\frac95,\frac{12}5\right)$ (indeed $AF=4$, so $\angle AFC=90^\circ$), and $D=(1,0)$.

Line $DF$: $(1+u,3u)$. Line $AB$: $\left(5-\frac{22}{5}t,\frac45t\right)$. Solving gives $t=\frac67$, $E=\left(\frac{43}{35},\frac{24}{35}\right)$. The shoelace formula for $C,D,E,B$:
$$\tfrac12\left|0+\tfrac{24}{35}+\left(\tfrac{43}{35}\cdot\tfrac45-\tfrac35\cdot\tfrac{24}{35}\right)+0\right|=\tfrac12\left(\tfrac{24}{35}+\tfrac{20}{35}\right)=\tfrac{22}{35}.$$

**Answer: 22/35**

hmmt-feb-2006-geo-05.title: Areas
hmmt-feb-2006-geo-05.body:
$[ACF]=\frac12\cdot3\cdot4=6$ (right angle at $F$, since $AF=4$). Because $CD=\frac15CA$, $[CDF]=\frac65$. Point $B$ divides $CF$ with $CB:BF=1:2$, so $[ABF]=\frac23\cdot6=4$. Menelaus (or mass points) gives $AE:EB=6:1$, so $[BEF]=\frac17[ABF]=\frac47$. The quadrilateral $CDEB$ is triangle $CDF$ with triangle $BEF$ removed, so its area is $\frac65-\frac47=\frac{22}{35}$.

**Answer: 22/35**

hmmt-feb-2006-geo-06.title: Centers along the angle bisector
hmmt-feb-2006-geo-06.body:
The small circle sits in the corner of an acute vertex $V$ (angle $\frac\pi4$), between the hypotenuse and a leg, touching the incircle. A circle of radius $\rho$ tangent to both sides of that angle has its center on the bisector at distance $\rho\csc\frac\pi8$ from $V$. The incircle and the small circle are externally tangent, with centers on the same bisector, so
$$(r-t)\csc\tfrac\pi8=r+t\ \Longrightarrow\ t=r\,\frac{\csc\frac\pi8-1}{\csc\frac\pi8+1}=r\,\frac{1-\sin\frac\pi8}{1+\sin\frac\pi8}.$$
Hence $rt=r^2\cdot\frac{1-\sin\frac\pi8}{1+\sin\frac\pi8}=\left(1+\sin\tfrac\pi8\right)\left(1-\sin\tfrac\pi8\right)=\cos^2\tfrac\pi8=\frac{1+\cos\frac\pi4}2=\frac{2+\sqrt2}4$.

**Answer: $\frac{2+\sqrt2}{4}$**

hmmt-feb-2006-geo-07.title: Tangent lengths and a right angle
hmmt-feb-2006-geo-07.body:
By symmetry the circles have equal radius $r$, and they touch on the axis of symmetry. Let $\omega_1$ with center $O_1$ touch $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ at $P,Q,R$. Then $PB=\frac12-r$ and $RC=3-r$, and by equal tangents $BQ=\frac12-r$, $QC=3-r$.

Since $O_1B$ and $O_1C$ bisect the angles at $B$ and $C$ (which sum to $180^\circ$), $\angle BO_1C=90^\circ$. With $O_1Q\perp BC$: $r^2=O_1Q^2=BQ\cdot QC=\left(\frac12-r\right)(3-r)=r^2-\frac72r+\frac32$. So $\frac72r=\frac32$ and $r=\frac37$.

**Answer: 3/7**

hmmt-feb-2006-geo-08.title: Reflect $D$ over $AB$
hmmt-feb-2006-geo-08.body:
Let $BD=x$ and reflect $D$ across line $AB$ to $D'$, which lies on line $BC$ with $D'D=2x$ and $AD'=AD$. Since $\angle BAD=\frac13\angle BAC$ we have $\angle DAC=2\angle BAD=\angle D'AD$, so $AD$ bisects $\angle D'AC$. By the angle bisector theorem in triangle $D'AC$: $\frac{D'D}{DC}=\frac{AD'}{AC}$, i.e. $2x=\frac{AD}{2}$, so $AD=4x$.

Also $AD^2=AB^2+x^2$ and $AB^2=AC^2-BC^2=4-(x+1)^2$, so $16x^2=x^2+4-(x+1)^2=3-2x$. Thus $16x^2+2x-3=0$, $(8x-3)(2x+1)=0$, and $x=\frac38$.

**Answer: 3/8**

hmmt-feb-2006-geo-09.title: Dihedral angle
hmmt-feb-2006-geo-09.body:
Let $O$ be the center of the sphere tangent to faces $ABC,ABD,BCD$ (so near vertex $B$). Let $P,Q$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $O$ to faces $ABC$ and $ABD$, and $R$ the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $AB$ (it is also the foot from $Q$). Then $OPRQ$ has right angles at $P$ and $Q$ with $OP=OQ=r$, and $\angle R$ is the dihedral angle of the tetrahedron, $\cos\angle R=\frac13$. Hence $QR=\sqrt2\,r$ and $BR=\sqrt6\,r$. By the same argument at $A$, $AB=2\sqrt6\,r+2r$, so $1=2r(\sqrt6+1)$ and $r=\frac{\sqrt6-1}{10}$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt6-1}{10}$**

hmmt-feb-2006-geo-09.title: Homothety
hmmt-feb-2006-geo-09.body:
The centers of the four spheres form a regular tetrahedron of side $2r$, homothetic to the big one with the same center, and its faces are at distance $r$ from the faces of the big tetrahedron. The inradius of a regular tetrahedron of side $s$ is $\frac{\sqrt6}{12}s$, so $\frac{\sqrt6}{12}\cdot2r=\frac{\sqrt6}{12}-r$. Thus $r\left(\frac{\sqrt6}{6}+1\right)=\frac{\sqrt6}{12}$ and $r=\frac{\sqrt6}{2(\sqrt6+6)}=\frac{\sqrt6-1}{10}$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt6-1}{10}$**

hmmt-feb-2006-geo-10.title: Coordinates
hmmt-feb-2006-geo-10.body:
Since $33^2+56^2=65^2$, $\angle C=90^\circ$, so the circumcircle has diameter $AB=65$. Put $C=(0,0)$, $A=(56,0)$, $B=(0,33)$; the circumcenter is the midpoint $\left(28,\frac{33}2\right)$, with radius $\frac{65}2$. The circle tangent to both legs inside the right angle has center $(r,r)$ and is internally tangent to the circumcircle:
$$(r-28)^2+\left(r-\tfrac{33}2\right)^2=\left(\tfrac{65}2-r\right)^2.$$
Expanding: $2r^2-89r+1056.25=r^2-65r+1056.25$, so $r^2-24r=0$ and $r=24$.

**Answer: 24**
